pattern.title: Donors decide what most of the money given to UN bodies pays for
pattern.summary:
A government can give a UN body or other multilateral organisation "core" money, which the organisation decides how to spend, or "earmarked" money, which the donor ties to a country, topic or project. The Financing the UN Development System report (Dag Hammarskjöld Foundation and UN MPTF Office, 2025) says earmarked money rose from 51% of all UN system funding in 2010 to 61% in 2023. In dollars that is $20.3 billion to $41 billion, down from $49.6 billion in 2022. Voluntary core money was $5.7 billion in 2023. The 2026 edition of the report gives $41.4 billion for 2024, again 61%, of $68.3 billion.

The UN Secretary-General's funding reports count only development and humanitarian work. For 2023 they put core money at 12.7% of voluntary contributions, or 18.8% with member states' dues added, and about 81% of funding as non-core. His 2019 report called 20.6% in 2017 an all-time low and said 2003 was the last year core passed 30% of voluntary development funding. Since the 2030 Agenda began, non-core money grew 44% after inflation and core 13%.

By organisation, 2023 revenue in the Financing report's Table 1 works out as follows (earmarked as a share of total revenue, worked out for this map): IOM $3.16 billion of $3.53 billion (90%), WFP $8.15 billion of $9.12 billion (89%), UNHCR $3.95 billion of $4.71 billion (84%), UNDP $4.82 billion of $5.93 billion (81%), UNICEF $7.14 billion of $8.93 billion (80%), WHO $2.56 billion of $3.34 billion (77%), FAO $1.81 billion of $2.40 billion (76%), UNFPA $1.09 billion of $1.68 billion (65%), UNEP $0.56 billion of $0.95 billion (59%). UNHCR's own report says its flexible money fell from 52% of its available resources in 2012 to 29% in 2020, then 36% in 2021. WFP wrote in 2019 that roughly 80% of its resources came tied to a specific activity. The WHO says 87% of its voluntary money in 2022-2023 was "tightly earmarked"; of the Gates Foundation's 640 grants to it from 2000 to 2024, worth $5.5 billion, about $3.2 billion went to polio (CIDRAP).

Across all multilateral bodies, OECD figures for its Development Assistance Committee donors put earmarked aid at 11% of their total aid in 2010, 21% at its 2022 peak and 18% in 2024. Core aid to multilateral bodies stayed close to 27% for most of the past decade and fell to 23% in 2024. An OECD article says these donors' earmarked money to multilateral bodies rose 42% in 2022 while core fell 6%. A dataset by Bernhard Reinsberg and colleagues counts 342,812 earmarked activities from nearly 50 donors to over 340 organisations between 1990 and 2020, and $33.0 billion of direct earmarked aid from the OECD committee's donors to operational organisations in 2020.
pattern.implications:
The OECD says extensive earmarking has been shown to split funding up, raise costs and reduce flexibility, and that working through shared bodies risks "becoming a channel for bilateral priorities." It also says earmarking can play "a constructive role" when it fits an organisation's mandate and the receiving country's priorities, and that donors favour it "to maximise control and visibility." The Secretary-General's 2025 report says tight earmarking raises costs and encourages agencies to compete, and that 57% of contributor governments surveyed in 2024 reported more competition for funding among UN bodies.

Donors' reply: contributor governments told the UN that "a lack of sufficient visibility to spending results is a significant disincentive for core contributions" (Secretary-General, para. 53). WFP's 2019 paper lists donors' constraints: legal requirements, domestic pressure over corruption and aid abuse, and demands for stricter reporting. Linnér and Reinsberg report the arguments made for earmarking: it brings in extra money, lets donors answer to voters and can support new ideas. The EU rarely gives core money because of its internal rules (Dag Hammarskjöld Foundation).

Agencies' reply: The UN MPTF Office's 2024 annual report says 67% of the $74.3 billion the UN raised in 2022 was earmarked and calls earmarking "a significant barrier to flexibility and responsiveness." Contributions to pooled funds, which several UN bodies share, doubled from $1.7 billion in 2016 to $3.4 billion in 2021, then fell to $2.8 billion in 2023 (Dag Hammarskjöld Foundation). Dominique Hyde, UNHCR's Director of External Relations, called flexible funding "the most powerful way to save lives." Peter Linnér writes that core money helps pay for audits, evaluations and financial management. Cintia Diaz-Herrera, a WHO external relations officer, was asked whether the Gates Foundation influences its agenda and said: "No, our agenda is very clear, and it has been for decades, before they existed as a foundation" (Devex, 2020). A Gates Foundation spokesperson, quoted by CIDRAP, said: "Philanthropy can make an important but limited contribution." Researchers at Queen Mary University of London say member states' failure to raise dues in line with the WHO's needs over four decades is why it depends on donors; member states have approved raising dues to cover 50% of its base budget by 2030.

The UN Funding Compact sets a target of a 30% core share of voluntary funding by 2027. Seven member states met that share in 2023. The share of governments' earmarked development money sent through pooled funds was 11.1% in 2023, against a 2027 target of 30% (Dag Hammarskjöld Foundation).

claims_per_author.claim: A good evaluation goes with more earmarked money from donors, about 49.2% more after three years (margin 2.6% to 116.8%), while evaluations show no link to core money.
claims_per_author.author_work: Reinsberg, Heinzel and Siauwijaya, Review of International Organizations, 2024

claims_per_author.claim: A 30-point rise in an organisation's earmarked share goes with a statistically significant fall in how well its systems and management run; at UNDP, comparing areas within countries, core money goes with gains in the Human Development Index and earmarked money shows no such effect.
claims_per_author.author_work: Linnér and Reinsberg, Global Governance Forum, 2026

claims_per_author.claim: Without money for audits, evaluations and oversight, the risks of corruption and waste would rise "multi-fold."
claims_per_author.author_work: Peter Linnér, in the Dag Hammarskjöld Foundation and MPTF Office report, 2025

claims_per_author.claim: Areas donors favour receive more than they need; member states' failure to raise dues is why the WHO depends on donors.
claims_per_author.author_work: Researchers at Queen Mary University of London (university named by CIDRAP), BMJ Global Health, 2025, as described in the BMJ Group press release

pattern.uncertain: The headline shares measure different things, so they should not be read as one line over time. 61% is earmarked money as a share of all UN system funding, dues included. About 81% is non-core within development and humanitarian contributions (Secretary-General; Linnér and Reinsberg give the same figure). The MPTF Office's 67% is for 2022 and matches $49.6 billion of $74.3 billion. The 20.6% for 2017 is a share of total funding for UN operational activities, and the 12.7% for 2023 is a share of voluntary funding only. The per-organisation percentages are worked out for this map from the extracted Table 1, not printed in the report; for WFP, UNICEF, UNDP and UNFPA blank cells were missing in the extract, so columns were placed by checking that they add to the printed total. The WHO's 77% is of revenue, against its own 87% of voluntary money; CIDRAP gives about 90% of 90%, and BMJ Group about 90% and almost all. The OECD figures cover its committee's donors only, and were read from a copy of the 2026 report whose text stopped short of the chapter tables, so the OECD's own by-organisation and by-donor earmarking figures (Figures 3.6-3.8) were not read. No figure was found for how much of the money given to development banks such as the World Bank is earmarked; the Center for Global Development gives earmarked aid as just under 30% of total multilateral spending, with no year stated. The Secretary-General's 2025 report was read as an advance unedited version. The OECD article on the 42% and 6% does not name the comparison year; its chart note covers the committee's donors in 2022 prices. Germany's "almost half" sits beside a Center for Global Development figure labelled 2020; the sentence itself gives no year. The Secretary-General's advance copy shows two document numbers on its cover, A/80/74/Add.1 and A/79/72/Add.1; the first is used here. The 49.2% in the Reinsberg paper has a wide margin, 2.6% to 116.8% at 95% confidence. The map arrow's end points are carried over from the earlier WHO-only version of this pattern. No case on this map is tied to this pattern.
